name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_SEQUENCING_MCQ_Q01 - Sequence of metals by increasing reducing power

questiontext.text:
Consider the standard reduction potentials of the following metals at \(298\text{ K}\):

(I) \(\mathrm{Ag}^+ / \mathrm{Ag}\) (\(E^\circ = +0.80\text{ V}\))
(II) \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} / \mathrm{Cu}\) (\(E^\circ = +0.34\text{ V}\))
(III) \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+} / \mathrm{Zn}\) (\(E^\circ = -0.76\text{ V}\))
(IV) \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+} / \mathrm{Mg}\) (\(E^\circ = -2.36\text{ V}\))
(V) \(\mathrm{K}^+ / \mathrm{K}\) (\(E^\circ = -2.93\text{ V}\))

Which of the following represents the correct sequence of these metals in order of their increasing reducing power?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle and Governing Relationship
The reducing power of a metal reflects its tendency to lose electrons (undergo oxidation) and reduce another species. In electrochemical thermodynamics, a lower (more negative) standard reduction potential \(E^\circ(\mathrm{M}^{n+}/\mathrm{M})\) indicates that the metal cation is harder to reduce, which conversely means the neutral metal \(\mathrm{M}\) oxidizes more readily. Therefore, standard reducing power increases as the standard reduction potential becomes increasingly negative.

Step 2: Comparison of Standard Reduction Potential Values
From the given electrochemical data at \(298\text{ K}\):
\(\bullet\) Silver: \(E^\circ(\mathrm{Ag}^+/\mathrm{Ag}) = +0.80\text{ V}\)
\(\bullet\) Copper: \(E^\circ(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}) = +0.34\text{ V}\)
\(\bullet\) Zinc: \(E^\circ(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}/\mathrm{Zn}) = -0.76\text{ V}\)
\(\bullet\) Magnesium: \(E^\circ(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+}/\mathrm{Mg}) = -2.36\text{ V}\)
\(\bullet\) Potassium: \(E^\circ(\mathrm{K}^+/\mathrm{K}) = -2.93\text{ V}\)
Arranging the standard reduction potentials in decreasing numerical order yields:
\(+0.80\text{ V} > +0.34\text{ V} > -0.76\text{ V} > -2.36\text{ V} > -2.93\text{ V}\).

Step 3: Determination of the Increasing Sequence
Because reducing power is inversely related to standard reduction potential, the least negative (most positive) potential corresponds to the weakest reducing agent, and the most negative potential corresponds to the strongest reducing agent:
\(\mathrm{Ag} < \mathrm{Cu} < \mathrm{Zn} < \mathrm{Mg} < \mathrm{K}\)
Matching the Roman numeral labels gives:
(I) \(\mathrm{Ag}\) < (II) \(\mathrm{Cu}\) < (III) \(\mathrm{Zn}\) < (IV) \(\mathrm{Mg}\) < (V) \(\mathrm{K}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Answer
Potassium readily donates its single valence electron (\(E^\circ = -2.93\text{ V}\)), making it the strongest reducing agent, whereas metallic silver possesses minimal tendency to lose electrons (\(E^\circ = +0.80\text{ V}\)). The strict order of increasing reducing power is (I) < (II) < (III) < (IV) < (V).
Final Conceptual Answer: (I) < (II) < (III) < (IV) < (V)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_SEQUENCING_MCQ_Q02 - Operational sequence with increasing opposing potential

questiontext.text:
In a standard Daniell cell (\(E_{\text{cell}} = 1.1\text{ V}\)), an opposing external potential (\(E_{\text{ext}}\)) is connected and gradually increased from \(0\text{ V}\) to values exceeding \(1.1\text{ V}\). Consider the following observed states and behaviors:

(I) Net cell current ceases completely, and no chemical reaction takes place at either electrode.
(II) Electrons flow naturally from zinc to copper, while zinc dissolves and copper deposits.
(III) Electron flow reverses from copper to zinc, causing zinc to deposit and copper to dissolve.
(IV) Forward current diminishes continuously as opposing potential increases, while electrons still flow from zinc to copper.

Which of the following presents the correct chronological sequence of these physical phenomena as \(E_{\text{ext}}\) is raised continuously from \(0\text{ V}\) upward?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Fundamental Electrochemical Operating Regimes of a Daniell Cell
A standard Daniell cell has an intrinsic cell electromotive force of \(E_{\text{cell}} = 1.1\text{ V}\). When an external opposing direct-current potential \(E_{\text{ext}}\) is applied, the effective net driving voltage governing current flow is \(V_{\text{net}} = E_{\text{cell}} - E_{\text{ext}}\).

Step 2: Analysis of Operational Stages with Increasing External Voltage
\(\bullet\) At \(E_{\text{ext}} = 0\text{ V}\), the cell operates under spontaneous galvanic conditions: electrons flow from the zinc rod (anode) to the copper rod (cathode) through the external circuit, accompanied by spontaneous dissolution of \(\mathrm{Zn}\) and deposition of \(\mathrm{Cu}\). This corresponds to statement (II).
\(\bullet\) When \(0\text{ V} < E_{\text{ext}} < 1.1\text{ V}\), the opposing potential reduces the net electromotive force. The forward current decreases progressively, yet current continues in the spontaneous galvanic direction, corresponding to statement (IV).
\(\bullet\) When \(E_{\text{ext}} = 1.1\text{ V}\), the opposing voltage exactly balances the cell potential (\(V_{\text{net}} = 0\)). Net current falls to zero, and all chemical changes at both electrodes cease entirely, corresponding to statement (I).
\(\bullet\) When \(E_{\text{ext}} > 1.1\text{ V}\), the external voltage overpowers the internal cell potential. The cell functions as an electrolytic cell: current is driven in reverse, electrons flow from copper to zinc, copper dissolves into solution, and zinc deposits on the zinc electrode, corresponding to statement (III).

Step 3: Chronological Assembly
As \(E_{\text{ext}}\) increases continuously from \(0\text{ V}\) through \(1.1\text{ V}\) and beyond, the stages occur in the sequence: (II) \(\rightarrow\) (IV) \(\rightarrow\) (I) \(\rightarrow\) (III).

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Answer
The transition follows spontaneous galvanic cell \(\rightarrow\) inhibited galvanic cell \(\rightarrow\) dynamic electrical equilibrium \(\rightarrow\) driven electrolytic cell. The sequence is strictly (II) \(\rightarrow\) (IV) \(\rightarrow\) (I) \(\rightarrow\) (III).
Final Conceptual Answer: (II) \(\rightarrow\) (IV) \(\rightarrow\) (I) \(\rightarrow\) (III)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_SEQUENCING_MCQ_Q03 - Increasing order of limiting molar conductivity

questiontext.text:
The limiting molar ionic conductivities (\(\lambda^\circ\)) at \(298\text{ K}\) from standard electrochemical data are given as follows:

\(\lambda^\circ(\mathrm{H}^+) = 349.6\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)
\(\lambda^\circ(\mathrm{Na}^+) = 50.1\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)
\(\lambda^\circ(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}) = 119.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)
\(\lambda^\circ(\mathrm{Cl}^-) = 76.3\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)
\(\lambda^\circ(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COO}^-) = 40.9\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\)

Consider the following four electrolytes:

(I) \(\mathrm{NaCl}\)
(II) \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COONa}\)
(III) \(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\)
(IV) \(\mathrm{HCl}\)

Which of the following represents the correct sequence of these electrolytes in order of increasing limiting molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_m^\circ\)) at \(298\text{ K}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Relevant Principle (Kohlrausch Law of Independent Migration of Ions)
According to Kohlrausch law, the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is equal to the sum of the individual limiting molar conductivities of its constituent cations and anions:
\[\Lambda_m^\circ = \nu_+ \lambda_+^\circ + \nu_- \lambda_-^\circ\] where \(\nu_+\) and \(\nu_-\) denote the stoichiometric numbers of cations and anions released per formula unit.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Calculation for Each Electrolyte
\(\bullet\) For (I) \(\mathrm{NaCl}\):
\[\Lambda_m^\circ(\mathrm{NaCl}) = \lambda^\circ(\mathrm{Na}^+) + \lambda^\circ(\mathrm{Cl}^-) = 50.1 + 76.3 = 126.4\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\]
\(\bullet\) For (II) \(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COONa}\):
\[\Lambda_m^\circ(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COONa}) = \lambda^\circ(\mathrm{Na}^+) + \lambda^\circ(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COO}^-) = 50.1 + 40.9 = 91.0\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\]
\(\bullet\) For (III) \(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\):
\[\Lambda_m^\circ(\mathrm{CaCl}_2) = \lambda^\circ(\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}) + 2\lambda^\circ(\mathrm{Cl}^-) = 119.0 + 2(76.3) = 119.0 + 152.6 = 271.6\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\]
\(\bullet\) For (IV) \(\mathrm{HCl}\):
\[\Lambda_m^\circ(\mathrm{HCl}) = \lambda^\circ(\mathrm{H}^+) + \lambda^\circ(\mathrm{Cl}^-) = 349.6 + 76.3 = 425.9\text{ S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 3: Ordering in Increasing Sequence
Comparing the calculated numerical values in units of \(\text{S cm}^2\text{ mol}^{-1}\):
\(91.0 < 126.4 < 271.6 < 425.9\)
Replacing with electrolyte labels:
\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{COONa}\) < \(\mathrm{NaCl}\) < \(\mathrm{CaCl}_2\) < \(\mathrm{HCl}\)
This corresponds directly to the sequence of Roman numerals: (II) < (I) < (III) < (IV).

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Answer
Sodium acetate has the lowest limiting molar conductivity due to the bulky, low-mobility acetate ion, whereas hydrochloric acid exhibits exceptionally high limiting molar conductivity due to the anomalously rapid Grotthuss proton-hopping mechanism of hydrogen ions. The verified order of increasing limiting molar conductivity is (II) < (I) < (III) < (IV).
Final Conceptual Answer: (II) < (I) < (III) < (IV)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_SEQUENCING_MCQ_Q04 - Procedural steps in measuring electrolytic conductivity

questiontext.text:
To accurately determine the molar conductivity (\(\Lambda_m\)) of an unknown electrolyte solution of known concentration \(c\) using a conductivity cell and a Wheatstone bridge setup, the following laboratory operations are executed:

(I) The cell constant (\(G^*\)) is calibrated by measuring the electrical resistance of a standard \(\mathrm{KCl}\) solution of known conductivity.
(II) The conductivity cell is thoroughly rinsed and filled with the test electrolytic solution of concentration \(c\).
(III) The variable standard resistor in the Wheatstone bridge is adjusted with an alternating current (AC) source until a null detector indicates electrical balance.
(IV) The solution conductivity (\(\kappa\)) is calculated from the measured resistance and cell constant, and subsequently divided by concentration \(c\) to obtain \(\Lambda_m\).

What is the correct chronological sequence of these experimental steps?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Experimental Context and Operational Logic
Determination of molar conductivity requires measurement of the test solution resistance in a conductivity cell. Because direct geometric measurement of electrode area \(A\) and inter-electrode distance \(l\) is unreliable, the cell constant \(G^* = l/A\) must be established first using a primary standard.

Step 2: Detailed Sequence of Experimental Stages
\(\bullet\) First, the conductivity cell is calibrated with a standard potassium chloride solution whose exact conductivity is known with high precision at a specified temperature. Measuring this standard resistance yields the precise cell constant \(G^* = \kappa_{\mathrm{KCl}} \cdot R_{\mathrm{KCl}}\), corresponding to operation (I).
\(\bullet\) Second, having calibrated the cell constant, the cell is emptied, thoroughly rinsed with conductivity water, and filled with the test electrolytic solution of known concentration \(c\), corresponding to operation (II).
\(\bullet\) Third, the filled cell is connected as one arm of a Wheatstone bridge powered by an alternating current (AC) source (to prevent electrolysis and electrode polarization). The variable precision resistor is adjusted until the null detector (such as headphones or an electronic indicator) detects zero sound or zero current, corresponding to operation (III).
\(\bullet\) Fourth, the measured equilibrium bridge resistance \(R\) is combined with the previously calibrated cell constant to compute electrolytic conductivity (\(\kappa = G^* / R\)), and finally molar conductivity is computed using \(\Lambda_m = \kappa / c\), corresponding to operation (IV).

Step 3: Chronological Assembly
The operations must logically proceed in the order: (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Answer
Calibration must precede measurement of the unknown; filling with the sample must precede bridge balancing; and balancing to obtain resistance must precede quantitative calculation of conductivity and molar conductivity. The sequence is strictly (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).
Final Conceptual Answer: (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_SEQUENCING_MCQ_Q05 - Chronological steps in atmospheric corrosion of iron

questiontext.text:
The electrochemical mechanism of atmospheric rusting of iron involves several sequential stages:

(I) Metallic iron undergoes oxidation at a specific anodic site, liberating electrons:
\[2\mathrm{Fe(s)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 4\mathrm{e}^-\]
(II) Released electrons migrate through the bulk metal to a cathodic site where dissolved atmospheric oxygen is reduced in the presence of \(\mathrm{H}^+\) ions:
\[\mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{g}) + 4\mathrm{H}^+(\mathrm{aq}) + 4\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O(l)}\]
(III) Ferrous ions diffuse across the aqueous surface layer and are further oxidized by atmospheric oxygen:
\[4\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{g}) + 4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O(l)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{O}_3(\mathrm{s}) + 8\mathrm{H}^+(\mathrm{aq})\]
(IV) Ferric oxide hydrates with surface water molecules to form rust:
\[\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{O}_3(\mathrm{s}) + x\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{O}_3 \cdot x\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O(s)}\]

Which of the following presents the correct chronological sequence of these electrochemical and chemical transformations during the rusting process?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Electrochemical Model of Rusting
Atmospheric corrosion of iron is an electrochemical phenomenon occurring in microscopic galvanic cells established on the metal surface in the presence of water containing dissolved carbonic acid or atmospheric gases supplying \(\mathrm{H}^+\) ions.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Chronological Progression
\(\bullet\) First, at an anodic site (often an area of mechanical stress or defect on the metal surface), iron atoms lose electrons to form soluble ferrous ions: \(2\mathrm{Fe(s)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + 4\mathrm{e}^-\) (\(E^\circ = -0.44\text{ V}\)), which is stage (I).
\(\bullet\) Second, the generated electrons travel through the conducting metal matrix to another region of the surface functioning as a cathode. In the presence of hydrogen ions provided by dissolved \(\mathrm{CO}_2\) or \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\), dissolved molecular oxygen accepts these electrons and is reduced to water: \(\mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{g}) + 4\mathrm{H}^+(\mathrm{aq}) + 4\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O(l)}\) (\(E^\circ = +1.23\text{ V}\)), which is stage (II).
\(\bullet\) Third, the resulting ferrous ions (\(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\)) migrate through the surface water film and encounter atmospheric oxygen, undergoing secondary non-electrochemical chemical oxidation to insoluble ferric oxide (\(\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)), regenerating hydrogen ions: \(4\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{g}) + 4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O(l)} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{O}_3(\mathrm{s}) + 8\mathrm{H}^+(\mathrm{aq})\), which is stage (III).
\(\bullet\) Fourth, the precipitated ferric oxide undergoes variable degree of hydration with available surface moisture to deposit as hydrated ferric oxide, commonly designated as rust: \(\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{O}_3 + x\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{O}_3 \cdot x\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\), which is stage (IV).

Step 3: Verification of Sequence
The electrochemical redox reaction between iron and oxygen must take place first to generate \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\) and consume electrons; this is followed by subsequent aerial oxidation of \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}\) to \(\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}\), and ultimate hydration to hydrated ferric oxide. The chronological progression is strictly (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Answer
The ordered pathway starts with anodic iron dissolution, proceeds through cathodic oxygen reduction, follows with secondary ferric precipitation, and concludes with rust hydration: (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).
Final Conceptual Answer: (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_SEQUENCING_MCQ_Q06 - Sequence of metals in salt displacement ability

questiontext.text:
Consider the standard reduction potentials of the following five metallic systems at \(298\text{ K}\):

\(\bullet\) \(\mathrm{Mg}^{2+} / \mathrm{Mg}\) (\(E^\circ = -2.36\text{ V}\))
\(\bullet\) \(\mathrm{Al}^{3+} / \mathrm{Al}\) (\(E^\circ = -1.66\text{ V}\))
\(\bullet\) \(\mathrm{Zn}^{2+} / \mathrm{Zn}\) (\(E^\circ = -0.76\text{ V}\))
\(\bullet\) \(\mathrm{Fe}^{2+} / \mathrm{Fe}\) (\(E^\circ = -0.44\text{ V}\))
\(\bullet\) \(\mathrm{Cu}^{2+} / \mathrm{Cu}\) (\(E^\circ = +0.34\text{ V}\))

A metal having a more negative standard reduction potential can displace a metal having a less negative or positive potential from its aqueous salt solution.

Which of the following represents the correct sequence of these metals arranged in the order in which each metal displaces all subsequent metals from their aqueous solutions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Governing Principle of Metal Displacement Reactions
A redox displacement reaction of the general form:
\[\mathrm{M}_1(\mathrm{s}) + \mathrm{M}_2^{n+}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{M}_1^{n+}(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{M}_2(\mathrm{s})\]
is thermodynamically spontaneous under standard conditions if the cell potential \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} > 0\). Since \(E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = E^\circ(\mathrm{M}_2^{n+}/\mathrm{M}_2) - E^\circ(\mathrm{M}_1^{n+}/\mathrm{M}_1)\), spontaneity requires that \(E^\circ(\mathrm{M}_1^{n+}/\mathrm{M}_1) < E^\circ(\mathrm{M}_2^{n+}/\mathrm{M}_2)\). Therefore, a metal with a more negative standard reduction potential acts as a stronger reducing agent and spontaneously displaces any metal with a less negative (or positive) reduction potential from aqueous solutions of its salts.

Step 2: Comparison of Standard Reduction Potentials
Arranging the given metal systems in increasing order of their standard reduction potentials (from most negative to positive):
\(\bullet\) \(\mathrm{Mg}\): \(E^\circ = -2.36\text{ V}\)
\(\bullet\) \(\mathrm{Al}\): \(E^\circ = -1.66\text{ V}\)
\(\bullet\) \(\mathrm{Zn}\): \(E^\circ = -0.76\text{ V}\)
\(\bullet\) \(\mathrm{Fe}\): \(E^\circ = -0.44\text{ V}\)
\(\bullet\) \(\mathrm{Cu}\): \(E^\circ = +0.34\text{ V}\)

Step 3: Verification of Mutual Displacement Power
\(\bullet\) \(\mathrm{Mg}\) (\(-2.36\text{ V}\)) displaces \(\mathrm{Al}\), \(\mathrm{Zn}\), \(\mathrm{Fe}\), and \(\mathrm{Cu}\).
\(\bullet\) \(\mathrm{Al}\) (\(-1.66\text{ V}\)) displaces \(\mathrm{Zn}\), \(\mathrm{Fe}\), and \(\mathrm{Cu}\).
\(\bullet\) \(\mathrm{Zn}\) (\(-0.76\text{ V}\)) displaces \(\mathrm{Fe}\) and \(\mathrm{Cu}\).
\(\bullet\) \(\mathrm{Fe}\) (\(-0.44\text{ V}\)) displaces \(\mathrm{Cu}\).
\(\bullet\) \(\mathrm{Cu}\) (\(+0.34\text{ V}\)) cannot displace any of the preceding metals.
Thus, the hierarchical displacement order where each metal displaces all subsequent metals is:
\(\mathrm{Mg} > \mathrm{Al} > \mathrm{Zn} > \mathrm{Fe} > \mathrm{Cu}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Answer
Magnesium has the highest oxidation tendency and copper has the lowest. The sequence where each preceding element displaces every succeeding element is \(\mathrm{Mg} > \mathrm{Al} > \mathrm{Zn} > \mathrm{Fe} > \mathrm{Cu}\).
Final Conceptual Answer: \(\mathrm{Mg} > \mathrm{Al} > \mathrm{Zn} > \mathrm{Fe} > \mathrm{Cu}\)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_SEQUENCING_MCQ_Q07 - Increasing charge required for electrochemical transformations

questiontext.text:
Consider the following stoichiometric electrochemical transformations:

(I) Complete oxidation of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{FeO}\) to \(\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{O}_3\)
(II) Complete oxidation of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) to \(\mathrm{O}_2\)
(III) Complete reduction of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Al}^{3+}\) to metallic \(\mathrm{Al}\)
(IV) Complete reduction of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^-\) to \(\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\) in acidic solution
(V) Complete reduction of \(1\text{ mol}\) of \(\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7^{2-}\) to \(\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}\) in acidic solution

Which of the following represents the correct sequence of these processes arranged in order of increasing quantity of electric charge (in Faradays) consumed per mole of the specified starting reactant?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Governing Relationship (Faraday's Laws of Electrolysis)
According to Faraday's laws of electrolysis, the total electric charge \(Q\) required to transform \(1\text{ mol}\) of a substance is directly proportional to the number of moles of electrons \(n\) exchanged in the balanced half-reaction:
\[Q = n \cdot F\] where \(F \approx 96487\text{ C mol}^{-1}\) is the Faraday constant. Hence, the required charge in Faradays equals the stoichiometric electron exchange coefficient \(n\).

Step 2: Analysis and Stoichiometric Calculation for Each Transformation
\(\bullet\) Transformation (I): In \(\mathrm{FeO}\), the oxidation state of iron is \(+2\). In \(\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{O}_3\), the oxidation state of iron is \(+3\). The balanced half-reaction per mole of \(\mathrm{FeO}\) is:
\[\mathrm{FeO} + \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{Fe}_2\mathrm{O}_3 + \mathrm{H}^+ + \mathrm{e}^-\]
Here, \(1\text{ mol}\) of electrons is transferred per mole of \(\mathrm{FeO}\). Therefore, \(Q_1 = 1\text{ F}\).
\(\bullet\) Transformation (II): In \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\), oxygen has an oxidation state of \(-2\), whereas in \(\mathrm{O}_2\) it is \(0\). The balanced half-reaction per mole of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) is:
\[\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O} \rightarrow \frac{1}{2}\mathrm{O}_2 + 2\mathrm{H}^+ + 2\mathrm{e}^-\]
Here, \(2\text{ mol}\) of electrons are released per mole of \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\). Therefore, \(Q_2 = 2\text{ F}\).
\(\bullet\) Transformation (III): The reduction of aluminium ion to metallic aluminium follows:
\[\mathrm{Al}^{3+} + 3\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Al}\]
Here, \(3\text{ mol}\) of electrons are required per mole of \(\mathrm{Al}^{3+}\). Therefore, \(Q_3 = 3\text{ F}\).
\(\bullet\) Transformation (IV): In permanganate (\(\mathrm{MnO}_4^-\), manganese has an oxidation state of \(+7\), and is reduced to \(\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}\) (\(+2\)) in acidic solution:
\[\mathrm{MnO}_4^- + 8\mathrm{H}^+ + 5\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Mn}^{2+} + 4\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]
Here, \(5\text{ mol}\) of electrons are consumed per mole of \(\mathrm{MnO}_4^-\). Therefore, \(Q_4 = 5\text{ F}\).
\(\bullet\) Transformation (V): In dichromate (\(\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7^{2-}\)), each chromium atom is in the \(+6\) oxidation state. The reduction of one mole of dichromate ions to \(\mathrm{Cr}^{3+}\) requires:
\[\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7^{2-} + 14\mathrm{H}^+ + 6\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr}^{3+} + 7\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\]
Here, \(6\text{ mol}\) of electrons are consumed per mole of \(\mathrm{Cr}_2\mathrm{O}_7^{2-}\). Therefore, \(Q_5 = 6\text{ F}\).

Step 3: Determination of the Increasing Sequence
Comparing the charge values in units of Faradays:
\(1\text{ F} < 2\text{ F} < 3\text{ F} < 5\text{ F} < 6\text{ F}\)
Matching the respective Roman numeral labels gives:
(I) < (II) < (III) < (IV) < (V).

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Answer
The stoichiometric requirement of electrons per mole of reactant increases strictly in the sequence of \(1\text{ F} \rightarrow 2\text{ F} \rightarrow 3\text{ F} \rightarrow 5\text{ F} \rightarrow 6\text{ F}\), establishing that the increasing sequence is (I) < (II) < (III) < (IV) < (V).
Final Conceptual Answer: (I) < (II) < (III) < (IV) < (V)

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_ELECTROCHEMISTRY_SEQUENCING_MCQ_Q08 - Sequence of processes in lead-acid battery discharge and recharge

questiontext.text:
Consider the complete operational cycle consisting of the discharge and subsequent recharging of a secondary lead storage battery. Examine the following chemical and physical events:

(I) Spontaneous oxidation of lead anode to \(\mathrm{PbSO}_4(\mathrm{s})\) and simultaneous reduction of \(\mathrm{PbO}_2\) cathode to \(\mathrm{PbSO}_4(\mathrm{s})\), consuming \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\).
(II) Progressive decrease in electrolyte density below \(1.20\text{ g cm}^{-3}\), signaling depletion of sulfuric acid.
(III) Application of an external electrical potential greater than cell potential with current driven in the reverse direction.
(IV) Electrolytic conversion of \(\mathrm{PbSO}_4(\mathrm{s})\) deposits back into spongy \(\mathrm{Pb}\) at the negative plate and \(\mathrm{PbO}_2\) at the positive plate, restoring sulfuric acid concentration.

Which of the following presents the correct chronological sequence of these events throughout the complete discharge and recharge cycle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Electrochemistry of the Lead Storage Battery
A lead storage battery functions as a galvanic cell during discharge and as an electrolytic cell during recharging.

Step 2: Analysis of the Full Operational Sequence
\(\bullet\) During spontaneous discharge (galvanic action), lead at the anode is oxidized: \(\mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}(\mathrm{aq}) \rightarrow \mathrm{PbSO}_4(\mathrm{s}) + 2\mathrm{e}^-\), while lead dioxide at the cathode is reduced: \(\mathrm{PbO}_2(\mathrm{s}) + 4\mathrm{H}^+(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{PbSO}_4(\mathrm{s}) + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O(l)}\). Both electrodes become coated with insoluble lead sulfate, and sulfuric acid is consumed. This corresponds to event (I).
\(\bullet\) As sulfuric acid (\(\text{density} \approx 1.30\text{ g cm}^{-3}\)) is continuously consumed to produce water (\(\text{density} \approx 1.00\text{ g cm}^{-3}\)), the density of the electrolyte drops progressively. When the density decreases below approximately \(1.20\text{ g cm}^{-3}\), the cell is substantially discharged and requires recharging. This corresponds to event (II).
\(\bullet\) To recharge the battery, it must be connected to an external direct-current power supply possessing a voltage greater than the battery's terminal voltage, thereby forcing electrons in the reverse direction into the cell. This corresponds to event (III).
\(\bullet\) Under this driven electrolytic regime, the electrode processes are reversed: \(\mathrm{PbSO}_4\) on the negative plates is reduced back to spongy metallic lead: \(\mathrm{PbSO}_4(\mathrm{s}) + 2\mathrm{e}^- \rightarrow \mathrm{Pb(s)} + \mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}(\mathrm{aq})\), while \(\mathrm{PbSO}_4\) on the positive plates is oxidized back to lead dioxide: \(\mathrm{PbSO}_4(\mathrm{s}) + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O(l)} \rightarrow \mathrm{PbO}_2(\mathrm{s}) + 4\mathrm{H}^+(\mathrm{aq}) + \mathrm{SO}_4^{2-}(\mathrm{aq}) + 2\mathrm{e}^-\), which regenerates \(\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{SO}_4\) and restores the original electrolyte density. This corresponds to event (IV).

Step 3: Chronological Assembly
The natural chronological sequence encompassing discharge, exhaustion, external power connection, and regeneration is: (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Answer
Discharge reactions produce lead sulfate and dilute the acid; this causes the density to drop; subsequently, an external charging potential is applied, driving the reverse electrolytic reactions that regenerate lead, lead dioxide, and concentrated sulfuric acid. The sequence is strictly (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV).
Final Conceptual Answer: (I) \(\rightarrow\) (II) \(\rightarrow\) (III) \(\rightarrow\) (IV)
